items.scene: At the end of dinner, the host glances at the clock and says, "It's getting late."
items.question: What is the host communicating beyond the literal words?
options: It is time for the guest to leave soon.
The host is asking about the weather.
items.why_this_case_matters: Classic conversational implicature: the extra meaning is inferred from context, not stated directly.

items.scene: A parent asks, "Did you finish all the cookies?" The child says, "I ate some."
items.question: What is implied?
options: Not all of the cookies were eaten.
The child is asking for more cookies.
The child is lying about eating cookies.
items.why_this_case_matters: Tests scalar implicature: a weaker term invites the stronger excluded alternative.

items.scene: A team lead says, "Could you send me the draft by noon?"
items.question: What is the team lead doing?
options: Implying the draft is already finished.
Saying noon is a bad time.
items.why_this_case_matters: This is indirect speech act, not implicature; the question targets the action performed.

items.scene: A manager asks whether all four reports are done. An employee replies, "Some of the reports are done," while knowing all four are done.
items.question: What is the main issue with this reply?
options: It is a misleading half-truth that can suggest the reports are incomplete.
It means exactly only some reports are done.
It is a polite warning to stop working.
It is a request for more time.
items.why_this_case_matters: This is a boundary case because the key issue is misleading expression, not a clean implicature alone.
